ai.literal: Greatness-yielding wealth even if obtaining, to others harmful things not doing is the blemishless people's principle.
ai.translation: Even if one were to obtain wealth that yields great glory, refraining from doing harmful things to others is the firm principle of those who are stainless.
ai.modern: சிறப்பைத் தரும் செல்வத்தைப் பெறுவதாக இருந்தாலும், மற்றவர்களுக்குத் துன்பம் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே குற்றமற்றவர்களின் கொள்கையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core principle of pure, faultless individuals. Even if they are offered immense wealth that brings supreme glory, they will not commit harmful deeds against others to acquire it. The word 'மாசற்றார்' refers to those free from the blemishes of the mind, and 'கோள்' represents their unshakeable vow or doctrine. Thus, harmlessness is placed above all worldly success and glory.

ai.literal: Even when [someone] does harmful things out of anger, not doing harmful things in return is the principle of those who are free from blemish.
ai.translation: Even when others do harm out of anger, refraining from doing harm in return is the principle of those who are free from blemish.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் கோபம்கொண்டு துன்பம் செய்தபோதிலும், அவருக்குத் திரும்பத் துன்பம் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே குற்றமற்றவர்களின் கொள்கையாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core standard of conduct for those who are pure and free from moral blemish (மாசற்றார்). The word 'கறுத்து' literally means 'having darkened' with rage, describing a person who acts out of blind anger to cause pain (இன்னா). Even under such extreme provocation (அக்கண்ணும்), a person of pure character must not retaliate with harm in return (மறுத்து இன்னா செய்யாமை). This steadfast refusal to return evil for evil is declared to be their defining principle (கோள்).

ai.literal: Without doing harm, even to those who harmed us, if one does evil things after, inescapable distress it will bring.
ai.translation: Even if others have caused us harm without any provocation, doing evil to them in return will bring us inescapable ruin.
ai.modern: நமக்கு ஒரு தீங்கும் செய்யாமல் நமக்குத் தீங்கு செய்தவர்க்கும் நாம் திரும்பத் தீங்கு செய்தால், அது நமக்குத் தப்பிக்க முடியாத பெரும் துன்பத்தைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the absolute principle of non-injury. It warns that even if someone harms us without any provocation, returning that harm will only result in inescapable misery for ourselves. The word 'செற்றார்' refers to those who harbor anger or cause harm, while 'உய்யா' means that which cannot be escaped or cured. Thus, the poet shows that retaliation is self-destructive, bringing unavoidable ruin to the one who seeks revenge.

ai.literal: Harmful things those who did, punishing them is, they to feel ashamed, good kindness having done, to leave it.
ai.translation: The way to punish those who have done harm to you is to make them feel ashamed by doing them a good turn and forgetting it.
ai.modern: நமக்குத் துன்பம் செய்தவரைத் தண்டிப்பது என்பது, அவர் வெட்கப்படும்படியாக அவருக்கு நல்ல நன்மைகளைச் செய்துவிட்டு அதனை மறந்துவிடுவது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the ultimate way to respond to those who cause us harm. Instead of seeking revenge or retaliating with violence, the poet suggests that the best punishment is to do them an act of pure goodness (நன்னயம்). When they receive kindness in return for their malice, they will feel deeply ashamed (நாண) of their actions. Finally, one must simply let the matter go (விடல்) without harboring any lingering resentment.

ai.literal: By knowledge what benefit is there, if one does not protect another's pain like one's own pain?
ai.translation: Of what use is a person's knowledge if they do not shield other living beings from pain as they would protect themselves from their own suffering?
ai.modern: மற்ற உயிர்களின் துன்பத்தைத் தன் துன்பத்தைப் போலக் கருதித் தடுத்துக் காப்பாற்றாவிட்டால், ஒருவன் பெற்ற அறிவினால் உண்டாகும் பயன் ஏதேனும் உண்டோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the true purpose of human intellect and wisdom. The author asks rhetorically what benefit can possibly come from knowledge if it does not lead to empathy. True wisdom must manifest as the ability to feel another's suffering as if it were one's own. If a person fails to protect others from pain, all their learning and intellect are rendered completely useless.

ai.literal: Painful things, as oneself realized, not practicing is required towards another doing.
ai.translation: One should not inflict those actions upon others which one has personally experienced and realized to be painful.
ai.modern: தனக்குத் துன்பம் தருபவை என்று தான் அனுபவித்து உணர்ந்த செயல்களை, மற்றவர்களுக்குச் செய்யாமல் தவிர்க்க வேண்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the core principle of empathy and non-injury. The word 'உணர்ந்தவை' refers to the painful experiences that a person has personally felt and understood to be harmful. The poet advises that once we realize a certain action causes suffering to us, we must make a conscious effort ('வேண்டும்') to avoid practicing ('துன்னாமை') those very actions towards others ('பிறன்கண் செயல்'). It is the ultimate test of moral conduct: treating others as we wish to be treated.

ai.literal: Even in the slightest measure, at all times, to anyone, with the mind arising, harmful deeds not doing is the foremost.
ai.translation: To refrain from doing even the slightest harm to anyone at any time, with a conscious mind, is the foremost of all virtues.
ai.modern: எவ்வளவு சிறியதானாலும், எப்போதும், யாருக்கும், தன் மனப்பூர்வமாகத் தீமையான செயல்களைச் செய்யாமல் இருப்பதே மிகச் சிறந்த அறமாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet defines the absolute standard of non-injury. The highest virtue ('தலை') is the complete avoidance of harmful deeds ('மாணா செய்யாமை'). This restraint must be total: it applies to even the smallest degree of harm ('எனைத்தானும்'), at all times ('எஞ்ஞான்றும்'), and towards all living beings ('யார்க்கும்'). Crucially, the phrase 'மனத்தான் ஆம்' emphasizes that this non-injury must stem from a sincere mental resolve, rather than mere outward compliance.

ai.literal: He who knows by himself what is painful to his own life, why indeed does he do painful things to other abiding lives?
ai.translation: How can a person, who knows from personal experience the pain inflicted on their own life, inflict pain on other living beings?
ai.modern: தன் உயிருக்குத் துன்பம் தருவது எது என்று தான் அனுபவித்து அறிந்தவன், மற்ற எளிய உயிர்களுக்குத் துன்பம் செய்ய நினைப்பது ஏனோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet establishes empathy as the foundation of non-injury. A person knows firsthand what causes pain and suffering to their own self ('தன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னாமை'). Having this direct, personal knowledge ('தான் அறிவான்'), it is incomprehensible ('என்கொலோ') why they would still choose to inflict similar suffering on other living creatures ('மன்னுயிர்க்கு இன்னா செயல்'). The word 'மன்னுயிர்' refers to the abiding, vulnerable lives of other living beings in the world. The poet uses a rhetorical question to urge the reader to use their own capacity for feeling pain as a guide to avoid harming others.

ai.literal: If one does harmful things to others in the forenoon, harmful things will come to themselves in the afternoon on their own.
ai.translation: If you do evil to others in the morning, evil will come to you on its own in the afternoon.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் மற்றவருக்குக் காலையில் துன்பம் செய்தால், அவருக்குத் துன்பமானது மாலையிலேயே தானாக வந்து சேரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses the natural division of a single day to illustrate the swift and inevitable return of one's actions. The terms 'முற்பகல்' (forenoon) and 'பிற்பகல்' (afternoon) serve as metaphors for the early and later stages of life, or simply the rapid cycle of cause and effect. The poet emphasizes that the harm we inflict on others ('பிறர்க்கு இன்னா') does not go unanswered; it returns to us ('தமக்கு இன்னா') automatically ('தாமே வரும்') without needing any external agent to deliver the punishment.

ai.literal: All suffering will become upon those who did suffering; they will not do suffering, those who desire the absence of suffering.
ai.translation: All suffering returns to those who cause suffering; therefore, those who desire to be free from suffering do not inflict pain on others.
ai.modern: துன்பங்கள் எல்லாம் பிறருக்குத் துன்பம் செய்தவர்களிடமே போய்ச் சேரும்; அதனால், தமக்குத் துன்பம் இல்லாதிருக்க விரும்புகின்றவர்கள் பிறருக்குத் துன்பம் செய்ய மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains the natural law of cause and effect regarding harm. The poet states that any suffering we inflict on others will eventually return to us. Therefore, those who wish to live a life free from pain and misery must refrain from causing harm to any living being. The repetition of the word 'nōy' (suffering/pain) emphasizes how closely our actions are linked to our own destiny.
